content: Educational programs designed to teach children with asthma how to manage their condition have been developed, but it remains uncertain whether these programs consistently lead to better health outcomes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of asthma self-management education in improving health outcomes for children. To conduct this evaluation, a systematic search was performed using the Cochrane Airways Group's Special Register of Controlled Trials and the PSYCHLIT database. Additionally, reference lists from relevant review articles were manually searched. The study included randomized and controlled clinical trials that focused on asthma self-management education for children and adolescents aged 2 to 18 years. Two independent reviewers assessed all the studies, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. When necessary, study authors were contacted to obtain missing data or to clarify methods. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the effects of different types and intensities of educational interventions, self-management strategies, trial designs, asthma severity levels, adequacy of follow-up, and overall study quality. Out of 45 identified trials, 32 studies involving a total of 3,706 children met the inclusion criteria. The results showed that asthma education programs led to moderate improvements in measures of lung function (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 0.75) and self-efficacy (SMD 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.57). These programs also resulted in modest reductions in the number of school days missed due to asthma (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.04), days with restricted activity (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.49 to -0.08), and emergency room visits (SMD -0.21, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.09). There was also a reduction in the number of nights disrupted by asthma symptoms when analyzed using a fixed-effects model, though this finding was not consistent when using a random-effects model. The benefits of these educational programs were more pronounced in children with moderate to severe asthma compared to those with mild to moderate asthma. Additionally, interventions that used peak flow monitoring strategies showed greater effects than those based on symptom monitoring. Improvements were observed within the first six months of the intervention, but for outcomes related to morbidity and healthcare utilization, the benefits were more evident after 12 months. The authors concluded that asthma self-management education programs for children lead to improvements across a variety of health outcomes. These programs, which focus on both the prevention and management of asthma attacks, should be integrated into routine asthma care. However, the study noted that there is limited evidence to determine the relative effectiveness of specific components of these educational programs due to a lack of direct comparisons. Future research should prioritize outcomes related to morbidity, functional status, and quality of life, and should include direct comparisons of the different components of asthma education interventions.
